questions.prompt: Explain the difference between LIFO and FIFO, and give one concrete iOS application example for each. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: LIFO stands for Last-In, First-Out, where the most recently added item is the first one removed, exemplified by UINavigationController pushing and popping view controllers. In contrast, FIFO stands for First-In, First-Out, where elements depart in their exact arrival order. A common iOS example of FIFO is a serial Grand Central Dispatch queue dispatching tasks sequentially.

rubric.criterion: Defines LIFO as Last-In First-Out and FIFO as First-In First-Out.
Provides a valid iOS example of LIFO like UINavigationController or undo stack.
Provides a valid iOS example of FIFO like GCD dispatch queues or download managers.

questions.prompt: Why is using Array.removeFirst() to implement a queue in Swift problematic for large datasets, and what are two better alternatives? Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, Array uses a contiguous memory buffer. Calling removeFirst() removes the element at index 0 and shifts every subsequent element one position to the left in O(n) time. Dequeuing n elements results in quadratic O(n^2) total runtime. Two efficient alternatives are implementing a two-stack queue for amortized O(1) performance or using Deque from Apple's swift-collections package.

rubric.criterion: Explains that removeFirst() takes O(n) time because all elements must shift left in memory.
Notes that dequeuing n elements from an array produces accidental O(n^2) quadratic time.
Suggests two valid O(1) alternatives such as two-stack queues, ring buffers, or Deque.

questions.prompt: Explain how a two-stack queue works and why its dequeue operation has an amortized O(1) time complexity. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: A two-stack queue uses an inbox stack for enqueuing and an outbox stack for dequeuing. When dequeuing, if outbox is empty, all elements from inbox are popped and pushed into outbox, reversing their order. While transferring n elements takes O(n) in the worst single call, each element is moved between stacks only once during its lifetime. This guarantees that the average cost per dequeue is amortized O(1).

rubric.criterion: Explains the role of inbox (for enqueue) and outbox (for dequeue) with order reversal.
Explains that transferring occurs only when outbox is empty.
Explains that each element is transferred at most once, establishing amortized O(1) time.

questions.prompt: Describe the algorithm to validate matching brackets like "()[]{}" with a stack, including how to handle invalid edge cases. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: To validate brackets, iterate through characters pushing opening brackets onto a stack. When encountering a closing bracket, pop the top element. Verify that it matches the opening type. Return false if the stack is empty or types mismatch. After processing the full string, check that stack.isEmpty returns true. This step rejects unclosed brackets.

rubric.criterion: Pushes opening brackets and pops to compare matching types upon closing brackets.
Returns false immediately if a closing bracket arrives with an empty stack or wrong type.
Verifies that stack.isEmpty at the end to catch unclosed opening brackets.

questions.prompt: Explain what a monotonic stack is and how it solves the Next Greater Element problem in linear O(n) time. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: A monotonic stack maintains its elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order. For Next Greater Element, we maintain a decreasing stack of indices. When an incoming number is greater than the element at `stack.last`, pop that index. Record the incoming number as its next greater element. Because each index is pushed once and popped at most once, total time is O(n).

rubric.criterion: Defines a monotonic stack as preserving strictly sorted element ordering.
Explains that smaller items are popped when a greater incoming value arrives.
Explains that each element is pushed once and popped at most once, yielding linear O(n) time.
